newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia minister preaches new reformist ideology.
newsitem.headline: Serbia minister preaches new reformist ideology.

text.p: Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Brko on Thursday rejected allegations that selling off state firms would lead to mass layoffs.
He said surplus labour existed anyway and free market reforms would

"Privatisation will not result in redundancies. We already have surplus labour. Any transformed firm means more efficiency and new jobs. But are we ready to do that? Are we ready for disillusion?" Beko told representatives of the Serbian power company Elektroprivreda Srbije's trade union.
EPS said earlier it planned to restructure and privatise.

It said it had asked the Belgrade-based Economics Institute and international auditors Deloitte & Touche to assess its capital and prepare a plan for its comprehensive restructuring and privatisation by the end of September.
EPS groups 23 companies and employs 61,500 workers.
"Reforms have no alternative. Your concern is not whether a strategic partner comes or whether the economy is privatised, but how you live," the minister said.
Beko insisted that most Serbian firms already had surplus labour and that an optimal employment rate was the only way to make the economy function.

"Only an economy with an optimum employment rate can satisfy its workers and interests of the state -- to become a good taxpayer so that the government generates sufficent revenues to finance its public spending," he said.
Beko also warned against prejudices towards reforms and privatisation.

"Those who have money should be allowed to come and invest and we shall have more and cheaper energy. EPS is not for sale but needs transformation to make it more efficient," he told the unios, which fear privatisation would trigger layoffs.
The government is applying reforms in doses depending on the economic situation, the minister added.
"But we must not allow pronounced social issues to overwhelm key aspects of reforms -- that our economy must become competitive and that we must conduct ownership transformation and adjustment.
"We shall have to pay the price for it."

Serbia's economy, legal system, social issues, infrastructure and monetary policy have been closely monitored by potential foreign investors following the 1995 end of nationalist wars in former Yugoslavia.

"Our attractiveness is there but we create the mood of the nation and the responsibility of the trade union lies exactly in whether we have a vision of a society we aim for, whether we shall be able to make it happen and whether we are ready to accept more radical changes to live better tomorrow," he said.
Beko said reforms did not only imply reformist legal framework but also a change of attitude.
"Now we need to change ideology, to push reforms forward and have no prejudices that foreign partners will come. Let them come and you will be better off."
